questions.question: Define transparent, translucent and opaque, giving two examples of each, and describe a simple test to classify a material.
questions.expected_answer: Transparent: lets almost all light through so objects are seen clearly (clear glass, clean water, clear plastic, air). Translucent: lets some light through but scatters it so objects behind are blurred (frosted glass, tracing paper, wax paper, lampshade, thin curtain). Opaque: lets no light through; light is reflected or absorbed (wood, brick, metal, cardboard, the body). Test: hold the material between a torch and a white screen; clear beam and torch visible through it = transparent; soft diffuse glow only = translucent; no light and a dark shadow = opaque.

questions.question: Explain how a shadow forms and how its size changes as an object is moved towards a lamp. Explain why outdoor shadows are long in the morning and point south at midday in South Africa.
questions.expected_answer: Light travels in straight lines; an opaque object blocks the light, and since light cannot bend round it, the region behind it receives no light from the source: a shadow with the outline shape of the object. Moving the object towards the lamp makes the shadow larger, because the rays spread more steeply past its edges; moving it towards the screen makes the shadow smaller. In the morning the Sun is low, so rays strike at a shallow angle and shadows are long (pointing west, away from the eastern Sun). In the Southern Hemisphere the midday Sun is in the northern sky, so shadows point roughly south and are shortest at midday.

questions.question: Distinguish between umbra and penumbra and explain why an extended source produces both. Explain how a solar eclipse and a lunar eclipse occur.
questions.expected_answer: Umbra: the completely dark central part of a shadow, where light from every part of the source is blocked. Penumbra: the partly lit outer region where light from only part of the source is blocked. An extended source has a size, so at some points on the screen light from part of the source is blocked and from part is not, giving a penumbra around the umbra; a point source gives only a sharp umbra. Solar eclipse: the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth; the Moon's umbra (total eclipse) and penumbra (partial eclipse) fall on Earth. Lunar eclipse: the Earth passes between the Sun and Moon (at full Moon); the Moon enters the Earth's shadow and turns red because the atmosphere bends red light into the shadow.
